description_full: Costamare Inc. owns and operates containerships and dry bulk vessels worldwide. Its containerships are chartered to liner companies providing transportation of cargoes. The company also charters dry bulk vessels to various customers providing worldwide transportation for dry bulk cargoes. As of February 24, 2026, it had a fleet of 79 containerships and 38 dry bulk vessels. The company was founded in 1974 and is based in Monaco.
ceo_bio: Mr. Konstantinos V. Konstantakopoulos | Chairman & CEO | Age 56
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $467K ranks in the above the sector median among Industrials peers, with revenue growing 13%/yr across its filed history. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture.
financial_summary: Costamare Inc. is a small-cap industrials business with a $1.6B market cap on $878M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -8% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 7% cost of capital, a 3-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.7× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 5.1×.

Shareholder yield of 4.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 62% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 4.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Revenue growth in the bottom decile of Industrials peers — losing share inside the profit pool
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Altman Z in the grey zone — financial health warrants monitoring
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 6% over 3 months
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 52% operating margin runs 43pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 4.67x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+33.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 7% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 7% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 26% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 0.79, it is more defensive than the market.
About $5.6M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 67% in the 2020 crash and 49% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 61% below its blended-model fair value of $33.93, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 51%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 5.2 vs 24.1 and EV/EBITDA 5.2 vs 13.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 7% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an EBIT/EV of 16.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $20.00 on average, 49% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 7.0%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.40).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.47x.
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 14pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 0.8% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.7x net debt to EBITDA ($539.1M of cash against $1.5B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 5.1x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -7.6% over 3 years and 13.8% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 38%).
Free cash flow has compounded 14.4% a year over five years.
own: Insiders own 61.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 35%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 1 sale over the past year, net $887K sold.
It returns 4.9% a year to shareholders (3.7% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 15 consecutive years, raising it 3.9% a year over the last five.
people: With about 1,880 employees, each generates about $467K of revenue, 1.3x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 12.7% a year across its filed history.
